questions.q: In text analysis, 'register' refers to
o: the level of formality and the language suited to a context
questions.why: Field, tenor and mode shape register.

questions.q: Lexis means
questions.why: Lexis = word choice.

questions.q: A declarative sentence
questions.why: The four sentence functions: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamative.

questions.q: An advertisement reads: 'Grab yours today, before they're gone!' Which feature is most prominent?
o: A passive construction that hides the agent
An imperative that creates urgency and addresses the reader directly
questions.why: 'Grab' is an imperative with implied second-person address, and 'before they're gone' adds time pressure. There is no question, passive or formality here.

questions.q: A company statement says: 'Mistakes were made.' What is the main effect of this agentless passive?
o: It avoids naming who was responsible
It makes the statement more informal and friendly
It stresses the speaker's personal guilt
It turns the statement into a question
questions.why: The passive lets the writer leave out the agent (who made the mistakes), which deflects blame. Naming oneself as the actor would need the active voice.

long.q: Analyse the language of an advertisement of your choice, focusing on how it persuades its audience. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: identifies audience, purpose and context
B1: analyses lexis with precise terminology
B1: analyses grammar or sentence structure for effect
B1: comments on structure and layout
B1: links every feature to its effect on the audience

long.q: Read this extract from a nature reserve's web page, then analyse how the writer uses language to engage readers. 'Step off the boardwalk and the city disappears. At Marshbrook, the only traffic is the heron's slow wingbeat over the reeds. Bring your boots, bring your curiosity, and leave your phone in your pocket: out here, the best notifications are birdsong. Open daily from dawn. Entry is free – but the memories are priceless.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: identifies audience (city-dwellers, families, day visitors) and the persuasive purpose of encouraging a visit
B1: imperatives ('Step off', 'Bring', 'leave') give direct address and make the visit feel immediate
B1: contrast of city and nature ('the city disappears', 'the only traffic is the heron's slow wingbeat') presents the reserve as an escape
B1: lexis from technology reused playfully ('notifications are birdsong'), a humorous appeal to a phone-using reader
B1: patterned structure: anaphora and a triad ('Bring your boots, bring your curiosity, and leave...') and the closing antithesis 'free'/'priceless' as a memorable slogan
B1: every feature named with accurate terminology and linked to its effect on the reader

long.q: Read this extract from a travel memoir, then analyse how the writer creates humour and a sense of the journey. 'I had been warned about the bus to Lindar. Nobody had warned me about the goat. It sat, regal and unbothered, in the seat reserved for elderly passengers, while its owner – a tiny woman in a purple shawl – apologised to no one. For six hours we climbed. The road narrowed; the drops deepened; the goat slept.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: first-person retrospective narrator with a dry, self-deprecating, conversational tone
B1: the parallel opening ('I had been warned... Nobody had warned me about the goat') sets up a comic anticlimax
B1: elevated lexis for an animal ('regal and unbothered') and the owner who 'apologised to no one' create incongruity
B1: short declarative 'For six hours we climbed.' and the asyndetic triad 'The road narrowed; the drops deepened; the goat slept.' build tension, then undercut it with bathos
B1: features analysed with precise terminology and linked to their effect on the reader, not just listed

long.q: Read this online restaurant review. 'Honestly? Best pizza I've had outside Naples. The crust – blistered, chewy, perfect. The service, sadly, was another story: we waited forty minutes for a table we'd booked. Would I go back? For the pizza, absolutely. For the waiting, never.' Identify three features of language or structure in the review and explain the effect of each.
scheme: B1: a first feature, e.g. minor sentences / questions answered by the writer ('Honestly?', 'Would I go back?')
B1: its effect, e.g. mimics speech, creating a chatty, trustworthy voice that engages the reader as if in conversation
B1: a second feature, e.g. the asyndetic list of adjectives 'blistered, chewy, perfect'
B1: its effect, e.g. sensory, enthusiastic praise building to the climax 'perfect'
B1: a third feature, e.g. the parallel, contrasting final sentences 'For the pizza, absolutely. For the waiting, never.'
B1: its effect, e.g. a balanced, memorable summary of the mixed verdict

long.q: Read this opening of a news report. 'Hundreds of residents were evacuated from homes in the Westbank district last night after the River Alde burst its banks following three days of record rainfall. Emergency services said no injuries had been reported, but warned that water levels could rise further before dawn.' Explain how the conventions of a news report shape the language and structure of this paragraph.
scheme: B1: the first sentence gives the key facts (who, what, where, when, why), the 'inverted pyramid' of news writing
B1: impersonal third-person register; the passive 'were evacuated' keeps the focus on the residents rather than who moved them
B1: attribution ('Emergency services said') through reported speech gives authority and credibility
B1: long complex sentences with subordinate clauses ('after...', 'following...') pack in a lot of information
B1: past tense for the events but the modal 'could rise' for what may follow, which creates urgency and keeps the story open

questions.q: A directed response asks you to
o: write a new text for a given audience and purpose, using a source
write a story of your choice
questions.why: You transform the source for a new context.

questions.q: In a directed response, what matters most?
o: Writing for the given audience, purpose and form
Using as many long words as possible
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some used a warning tone when the task asked for advice or persuasion.

questions.q: What should the comparison with the original text do?
o: Analyse how language choices differ and why, with examples
questions.why: Examiners (2023): weaker comparisons summarised content with few examples.

questions.q: You must turn a formal travel-guide extract into a blog post for teenagers. Which change is most appropriate?
o: Keep every formal phrase so that nothing is lost
Turn the information into a poem
Replace the information with a story about yourself
Adopt a conversational first-person voice with direct address, while keeping the key information
questions.why: A directed response reworks the source's content for a new audience, purpose and form. The register changes, but the relevant information must remain.

questions.q: Which is a typical convention of a speech rather than a written article?
o: Direct address to listeners and spoken signposting such as 'Let me turn now to...'
questions.why: Speeches are designed to be heard, so they use direct address and oral signposting to guide listeners. Headings and footnotes are features of written layout.

long.q: Read this text from a museum leaflet. 'The Hallam Textile Museum occupies a former spinning mill built in 1832. Visitors may examine working looms, a reconstructed workers' cottage and an archive of pattern books dating from the eighteenth century. Guided tours are conducted hourly. Photography is permitted in all galleries except the archive.' Using this information, write the opening of a podcast script (about 150 words) introducing the museum to listeners aged 11–13. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: podcast conventions: greeting, presenter introduction, direct address to listeners, possibly cues such as [sound of looms]
B1: register suited to 11–13-year-olds: lively, informal, accessible lexis (no 'occupies', 'conducted', 'permitted')
B1: the key facts kept accurately: 1832 mill, working looms, workers' cottage, old pattern books, hourly tours, no photos in the archive
B1: content selected and reshaped to interest the audience, not copied in the original order
B1: about 150 words, fluent and accurate

long.q: A council notice reads: 'Notice: Elm Park will be closed to the public from 3 to 17 June to allow essential drainage works to be carried out. The council apologises for any inconvenience caused.' A student rewrote it as a post for a local dog-walkers' blog: 'Bad news, dog people – Elm Park's shutting for two whole weeks (3–17 June) while they sort out the drains. Time to scout out a new route! Any suggestions? Drop them in the comments.' Compare the language and style of the two texts. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: register: the notice is formal and impersonal; the blog is informal and personal, addressing 'dog people' directly
B1: grammar: the agentless passive 'to be carried out' (institutional distance) against the active, colloquial 'they sort out'
B1: lexis: formal, Latinate 'essential drainage works', 'inconvenience' against phrasal verbs and colloquialisms ('shutting', 'sort out', 'scout out')
B1: purpose: the notice informs and apologises; the blog informs and builds community through questions and imperatives ('Any suggestions?', 'Drop them in the comments')
B1: form and graphology: the heading 'Notice:' against dashes, an exclamation, contraction ('Park's') and online conventions ('comments')
B1: a point-by-point comparison with terminology and effects, not two separate descriptions

long.q: A hotel guest posted this online review: 'Two stars, and that's generous. Booked a 'sea view' room – got a view of the car park bins. The aircon rattled all night like a dying lawnmower. Breakfast ran out of eggs at 8.15. Staff were lovely, to be fair, but they can't fix everything with a smile.' Using the review, write the guest's formal letter of complaint to the hotel manager (about 200 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: letter conventions: formal salutation, the dates of the stay or booking reference, a formal sign-off
B1: a measured, formal register: sarcasm and comic images ('dying lawnmower') removed or turned into plain statements
B1: all three complaints transferred accurately: the room had no sea view, the air conditioning was noisy, breakfast ran out
B1: the praise of the staff kept, which makes the complaint sound fair and credible
B1: a clear, reasonable request for action (an explanation, a partial refund) that suits the purpose

long.q: This sentence comes from a scientific report: 'Participants (n = 240) who engaged in moderate aerobic exercise for 150 minutes per week exhibited a statistically significant reduction in self-reported anxiety scores relative to the control group.' Explain three changes you would make to turn it into text for a leaflet for the general public, giving a reason for each.
scheme: B1: a change: replace technical lexis ('n = 240', 'statistically significant', 'control group') with everyday words
B1: reason: general readers lack specialist knowledge, so clarity matters more than precision
B1: a change: break the long nominalised sentence into short sentences in the active voice, with direct address ('you')
B1: reason: this makes the text easier to read and more personal and engaging
B1: a change: add practical, persuasive advice and layout, e.g. a heading and 'Try 30 minutes a day, five days a week'
B1: reason: the purpose shifts from reporting findings to encouraging the reader to act

long.q: A press release reads: 'Riverton Youth Orchestra will perform its first-ever concert at the City Hall on Saturday 14 March. The 60 musicians, aged 12 to 18, have rehearsed weekly for eight months under conductor Alma Reyes. Tickets (£5) are available online; all proceeds go to music lessons for local children.' Write the diary entry (about 150 words) of a 15-year-old violinist on the night of the concert. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: diary conventions: date, first person, reflective, written for a private audience
B1: a convincing personal voice (nerves, excitement, relief) in a register suited to a 15-year-old
B1: details from the press release used accurately and naturally (first concert, City Hall, 60 players, eight months of rehearsals, Alma Reyes, money for lessons)
B1: the information transformed into experience rather than listed as facts
B1: about 150 words, controlled and accurate

questions.q: A reflective commentary should explain
o: the language choices you made and why
questions.why: It links your choices to audience and purpose.

questions.q: A review task asks about a trip. What is a weakness?
o: Writing a recount with no evaluation
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many reviews read like holiday accounts.

questions.q: A story opening is set. What should you avoid?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some wrote a complete story instead of an opening.

questions.q: Which sentence from a reflective commentary is most effective?
o: I used lots of good techniques to make my writing interesting.
My story is about a girl who gets lost in a forest.
I used the minor sentence 'Silence.' to slow the pace and mirror the narrator's shock.
I think my writing turned out quite well.
questions.why: It names a precise feature, quotes it and explains its effect in context. The others are vague, retell content or simply give an opinion.

questions.q: In a review, which sentence best combines description with evaluation?
o: We went to the restaurant on Friday at seven o'clock.
The restaurant has twelve tables and a blue door.
Everyone should eat out more often.
The lamb curry, rich with cardamom but let down by tough meat, was the evening's near-miss.
questions.why: A review needs judgement as well as detail; this sentence describes the dish precisely and evaluates it. The others are recount, bare description or an unrelated opinion.

long.q: Write the opening of a short story (about 400 words) in which a character returns to a place after many years away. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: an opening that hooks the reader, e.g. starting in the middle of the action or with an intriguing detail
B1: a clear narrative voice and a consistent point of view
B1: setting built from a few precise, selective details rather than lists
B1: the past hinted at without over-explaining (showing, not telling)
B1: varied sentence lengths and paragraphing to control pace
B1: about 400 words, with accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Write a reflective commentary (about 150 words) on a piece of shorter writing you have produced, explaining how your language choices suit its audience and purpose. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: identifies the audience, purpose, form and context and how they shaped the writing
B1: discusses specific lexical choices, quoted briefly, with their intended effect
B1: discusses grammatical or structural choices (sentence types, tense, paragraphing, openings) with their effect
B1: uses accurate linguistic terminology throughout
B1: explains why choices were made, not just what they are, within the word limit

long.q: Write a review (about 400 words) of a café or restaurant you know for a website run by students. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: review conventions: name and context of the place, an overall verdict or rating
B1: description and evaluation combined (what it was like and how good it was)
B1: a lively voice and register suited to students: informal but controlled
B1: specific, vivid detail (a dish, the service, the price) rather than general praise
B1: about 400 words, accurate and fluent

long.q: Write a speech (about 400 words) to be given by a student at a school leavers' ceremony. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: spoken conventions: address to the audience, signposting, direct address ('we', 'you')
B1: rhetorical devices used for a purpose, e.g. anecdote, triads, rhetorical questions
B1: a tone that balances humour and sentiment, suited to the occasion
B1: a clear structure: engaging opening, development, memorable close
B1: about 400 words, accurate and fluent

long.q: A student wrote this opening to a descriptive piece: 'Rain. Again. It drummed on the tin roof of the bus shelter, a thousand impatient fingers, while the 7.42 failed – as usual – to appear.' Write the part of a reflective commentary in which the student explains three of the language choices in this opening.
scheme: B1: identifies the minor sentences 'Rain. Again.'
B1: explains the effect: an immediate weary, resigned tone and a sense of monotony
B1: identifies the metaphor 'a thousand impatient fingers' (personification of the rain)
B1: explains the effect: sound imagery that mirrors the narrator's own impatience
B1: identifies the parenthesis '– as usual –'
B1: explains the effect: a wry, conversational aside that shows the narrator's frustration and humour

questions.q: Writing for a specified audience means
o: adapting vocabulary, tone and structure to that audience
using as many long words as possible
questions.why: Audience shapes every choice.

questions.q: Which is a common sentence error to avoid in extended writing?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): comma splicing and fragments recurred.

questions.q: Which helps an extended piece of writing most?
o: A clear structure planned around the purpose and audience
questions.why: Examiners (2023): stronger responses were structured deliberately, not just chronologically.

questions.q: Which is the most effective opening for a magazine article arguing that cars should be banned from city centres?
o: Imagine walking down your high street and hearing birdsong instead of engines.
In this article I will talk about cars.
Cars were invented in the late nineteenth century.
There are many points of view on this topic.
questions.why: It engages the reader directly and creates an appealing image that supports the argument. The others are flat announcements, irrelevant facts or non-committal.

questions.q: Which technique best creates cohesion between paragraphs?
o: Changing the font for each paragraph
Topic sentences and discourse markers that link back to the previous point
Repeating the title at the start of each paragraph
questions.why: Cohesion comes from linguistic links such as discourse markers ('However', 'This suggests') and reference back to earlier ideas, so the argument flows.

long.q: Write an opinion article (600–900 words) for a national newspaper arguing for or against a four-day school week. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear line of argument, sustained throughout
B1: points developed with evidence, examples or anecdote
B1: an opposing view raised and answered
B1: article conventions: headline, engaging opening, a confident columnist's voice
B1: register suited to a broad adult readership
B1: accurate, varied and controlled expression within the word range

long.q: Write a short story (600–900 words) called 'The Last Train'. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: an opening that engages and establishes the situation quickly
B1: a coherent plot with tension and a shaped, convincing ending
B1: characters developed through dialogue and action
B1: setting and atmosphere that support the mood
B1: narrative techniques (viewpoint, flashback, pacing) used deliberately
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, including dialogue

long.q: Write a speech (600–900 words) for a youth conference called 'Why my generation should care about local politics'. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear argument that addresses the title directly
B1: reasons supported by concrete local examples (transport, parks, housing, services)
B1: likely objections ('it makes no difference', 'politics is boring') anticipated and answered
B1: rhetorical techniques suited to speech: direct address, repetition, a call to action
B1: register suited to an audience of young people
B1: a structured, controlled and accurate piece within the word range

long.q: Write a descriptive piece (600–900 words) called 'The Empty Theatre'. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: description sustained rather than drifting into a story
B1: precise sensory detail and original imagery, avoiding cliché
B1: a deliberate structure, e.g. moving through the space or through time
B1: a range of sentence structures used for effect
B1: accurate, ambitious vocabulary and controlled expression

long.q: Write the script of a podcast episode (600–900 words) for adult listeners exploring the question 'Is boredom good for us?' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: podcast conventions: introduction, direct address, a conversational spoken style
B1: an exploratory, discursive structure that considers more than one view
B1: ideas developed with examples or anecdote (creativity, phones, childhood)
B1: an engaging tone suited to adult listeners
B1: accurate, varied expression within the word range

questions.q: Borrowing (as in 'bungalow' from Hindi) is an example of
questions.why: Words enter English from other languages.

questions.q: When a word's meaning becomes more negative over time, this is
questions.why: e.g. 'silly' once meant blessed.

questions.q: Which is a theory of language change?
questions.why: Others: S-curve, wave model, random fluctuation.

questions.q: The word 'nice' once meant 'foolish' but now means 'pleasant'. This is an example of
questions.why: Amelioration is when a word's meaning becomes more positive over time. Pejoration is the opposite, and narrowing is when a meaning becomes more specific.

questions.q: Which word was formed by blending?
questions.why: A blend joins parts of two words, as in sm(oke) + (f)og. NASA is an acronym, bus is a clipping, and kindergarten is a borrowing from German.

long.q: Read this shop advertisement, written in the style of the eighteenth century. 'To the Publick. – Mr. Haywood begs leave to acquaint the Nobility and Gentry, that he hath lately open'd a Shop in Bridge-street, where may be had the finest Teas, Coffee and Chocolate, at the most reasonable Prices.' Identify and explain four features that show this is not Present-Day English.
scheme: B1: capital letters on many common nouns ('Shop', 'Teas', 'Prices')
B1: explained: a printing convention of the period, later standardised so only proper nouns are capitalised
B1: spelling 'Publick' with final -ck
B1: explained: spelling was later standardised to 'public'
B1: the elided past form 'open'd' and the verb form 'hath'
B1: explained: '-ed' is now written in full and the third-person -th ending was replaced by -s ('has')
B1: deferential formulae and word order ('begs leave to acquaint', 'Nobility and Gentry', 'where may be had')
B1: explained: reflects a rigid social hierarchy and older syntax; the inverted passive would now be 'where you can buy'

long.q: Corpus data show that 'motorcar' rose in use from the 1890s, peaked around 1920 and had almost disappeared by 1980, while 'car' rose steadily from 1900 and dominated after about 1930. Explain what these data suggest about how language changes.
scheme: B1: a new technology created a lexical gap, filled by a compound (motor + car)
B1: once the technology was everyday, the shorter form took over (economy, the principle of least effort)
B1: 'car' already existed (a cart, carriage or railway car) and narrowed to mean a motor vehicle: semantic change
B1: the timing links to mass car ownership in the early twentieth century: social change drives lexical change

long.q: Explain, with an example of each, three processes of semantic change.
scheme: B1: broadening: a word's meaning becomes more general
B1: example, e.g. 'holiday', once a 'holy day', now any day off work
B1: narrowing: a word's meaning becomes more specific
B1: example, e.g. 'meat', once any food, now animal flesh
B1: pejoration or amelioration: a meaning becomes more negative or more positive
B1: example, e.g. 'silly', once 'blessed' or 'innocent', now 'foolish' (pejoration)

long.q: Explain the difference between prescriptive and descriptive attitudes to language change, referring to Aitchison's metaphors.
scheme: B1: prescriptivism: judges change as decline and lays down rules of 'correct' usage (e.g. eighteenth-century grammarians such as Lowth)
B1: descriptivism: records how language is used without judging it, and treats change as natural
B1: Aitchison's 'damp spoon' syndrome: the belief that change comes from laziness or sloppiness
B1: Aitchison's 'crumbling castle': the belief in a past golden age from which the language has decayed
B1: Aitchison's own view: change is neither progress nor decay, and these fears are myths

long.q: Name the word-formation process behind each of these words: (a) radar (b) edit (from 'editor') (c) vlog (d) to google (e) flu (f) tsunami.
scheme: B1: (a) acronym (RAdio Detection And Ranging)
B1: (b) back-formation (a verb formed by removing what looks like a suffix)
B1: (c) blending (video + blog)
B1: (d) conversion (a proper noun used as a verb)
B1: (e) clipping (from 'influenza')
B1: (f) borrowing (from Japanese)
long.ans: acronym; back-formation; blending; conversion; clipping; borrowing

questions.q: 'Holophrastic' speech is
o: one word used to express a whole idea
questions.why: e.g. 'juice' meaning 'I want juice'.

questions.q: Overgeneralisation, as in 'goed', shows that children
questions.why: Applying a rule where it doesn't fit shows rule-learning.

questions.q: Which theorist argued children are born with a language acquisition device?
questions.why: Use child-language data to support or challenge theories.

questions.q: A child says 'Mummy sock', meaning 'That is Mummy's sock'. Which stage is this typical of?
questions.why: Two content words combined to express a relationship (here, possession) is typical of the two-word stage, at around 18 to 24 months.

questions.q: Bruner's Language Acquisition Support System (LASS) emphasises
o: an innate grammar device in the brain
the role of caregivers' interaction and routines in supporting language learning
the order of cognitive stages a child passes through
questions.why: Bruner stressed scaffolding by caregivers, for example through routines and shared reading, as a social answer to Chomsky's innate LAD. Imitation and reinforcement is Skinner's view.

long.q: A child of 2 years says 'daddy car go'. Comment on what this shows about the child's language development.
scheme: B1: telegraphic stage (about 2;0–2;6)
B1: content words kept; function words (determiners, auxiliaries) omitted
B1: correct subject–object–verb meaning order
B1: links to a theory, e.g. Brown's stages or Chomsky's LAD

long.q: Read this transcript of a child aged 2;6 talking to her mother. Child: I goed to park. Mother: You went to the park? Who did you go with? Child: Nana. Nana pushed me on swing. Mother: Did she? Was it a big swing? Child: Big big swing! Two foots on ground. Analyse what the transcript shows about the child's language development and the role of the caregiver.
scheme: B1: 'goed' overgeneralises the regular past -ed rule: a virtuous error showing a rule has been learned, not imitated
B1: 'foots' overgeneralises the regular plural -s in the same way
B1: determiners omitted ('to park', 'on swing'): function words still missing as the child moves beyond the telegraphic stage
B1: 'Nana pushed me on swing' is a full subject–verb–object clause with a correct past tense: syntax developing
B1: the mother recasts ('You went to the park?') without direct correction, and the child does not take up the form at once (evidence against pure imitation)
B1: the mother's questions scaffold the conversation and model turn-taking (child-directed speech, Bruner's LASS)

long.q: Describe, with an example of each, three phonological strategies young children use to simplify words.
scheme: B1: deletion, e.g. dropping a final consonant
B1: example, e.g. 'ca' for 'cat'
B1: consonant cluster reduction
B1: example, e.g. 'poon' for 'spoon'
B1: substitution (or reduplication)
B1: example, e.g. 'wabbit' for 'rabbit' (or 'baba' for 'bottle')

long.q: Evaluate the view that children acquire language mainly through imitation.
scheme: B1: the behaviourist view (Skinner): language is learned through imitation and reinforcement
B1: support: children acquire the accent, dialect and vocabulary of those around them
B1: against: virtuous errors such as 'goed' or 'mouses', which no adult models
B1: against: children often resist explicit correction and keep their own form
B1: the nativist alternative: Chomsky's LAD and the 'poverty of the stimulus'
B1: the interactionist alternative: Bruner's LASS and caregiver scaffolding
B1: the cognitive alternative: Piaget, where language follows cognitive development
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. imitation explains lexis and accent but not the acquisition of grammar

long.q: Using Halliday's functions of language, identify the function of each utterance by a three-year-old: (a) 'Want juice!' (b) 'Don't touch my tower!' (c) 'Hello, Nana!' (d) 'I'm a big girl now.' (e) 'Why is the moon following us?'
scheme: B1: (a) instrumental: getting a need met
B1: (b) regulatory: controlling someone else's behaviour
B1: (c) interactional: forming and keeping relationships
B1: (d) personal: expressing identity and feelings
B1: (e) heuristic: finding out about the world

questions.q: A pidgin is
o: a simplified contact language with no native speakers
questions.why: When it gains native speakers it becomes a creole.

questions.q: What is Schneider's dynamic model about?
o: Stages in how new varieties of English develop in former colonies
questions.why: Examiners (2023): RP was often wrongly described as the British standard.

questions.q: What does 'acrolect' mean?
o: The most prestigious variety, closest to the standard
questions.why: Basilect is furthest from it; mesolect is between.

questions.q: In Kachru's three-circle model, which circle includes India and Nigeria?
questions.why: The Outer Circle covers countries where English has an official or institutional role after colonisation. The Inner Circle is where it is the main first language, and the Expanding Circle is where it is learned as a foreign language.

questions.q: A creole differs from a pidgin because a creole
o: is a regional variety of Standard English
has native speakers and has become a community's first language
questions.why: When children grow up speaking a pidgin as their first language, it expands and becomes a creole with a fuller grammar and vocabulary.

long.q: Explain Kachru's three-circle model of English, giving an example country for each circle.
scheme: B1: inner circle: English is the first language for most people; 'norm-providing'
B1: example, e.g. the UK, the USA or Australia
B1: outer circle: English is an official or second language, usually because of colonial history; 'norm-developing'
B1: example, e.g. India, Nigeria or Singapore
B1: expanding circle: English is learned as a foreign language for international use; 'norm-dependent'
B1: example, e.g. China, Japan or Brazil

long.q: Evaluate Kachru's three-circle model as a description of how English is used today.
scheme: B1: strength: simple and clear, showing the historical spread of English
B1: strength: treats outer-circle varieties (e.g. Indian English) as legitimate Englishes, not errors
B1: weakness: based on nation-states, so ignores variation inside countries (proficiency in India varies hugely; many people in inner-circle countries are not first-language speakers)
B1: weakness: expanding-circle speakers now outnumber first-language speakers and use English as a lingua franca without following inner-circle norms
B1: other models compared, e.g. Schneider's dynamic model or Modiano's proficiency-based model
B1: a reasoned judgement on how useful the model still is

long.q: Explain how a pidgin may develop into a creole.
scheme: B1: a pidgin arises from contact between groups with no shared language (trade, plantations, colonisation)
B1: a pidgin has a small vocabulary drawn mostly from one dominant (lexifier) language, simple grammar and no native speakers
B1: creolisation: children grow up speaking it as their first language
B1: the creole expands its vocabulary and grammar (e.g. tense and aspect markers) to serve every function of a full language
B1: an example, e.g. Tok Pisin in Papua New Guinea or Jamaican Creole

long.q: Read this exchange in Singapore Colloquial English (Singlish): 'Eh, you going canteen or not? Wait ah, I need to finish this first. Later we go together lah.' Identify and explain three features of this variety.
scheme: B1: discourse particles 'ah' and 'lah'
B1: explained: borrowed from Chinese varieties or Malay; they express attitude, soften or add emphasis
B1: the auxiliary 'are' omitted ('you going')
B1: explained: influence of substrate languages without a copula; a simplification found in contact varieties
B1: the question form 'going canteen or not?' (with no preposition or article)
B1: explained: modelled on the Chinese 'A-not-A' question; the dropped 'to the' shows simplification

long.q: 'English as a global language threatens the world's linguistic diversity.' Discuss this view. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: explains language endangerment and English's dominance in business, education, science and the internet
B1: an example, e.g. families choosing English-medium schooling over local languages
B1: a theory, e.g. Phillipson's 'linguistic imperialism'
B1: counter: many languages are lost to national or regional languages (Mandarin, Spanish, Swahili), not to English
B1: counter: English is often added to people's languages (bilingualism), not a replacement
B1: counter: English itself diversifies into new Englishes; revitalisation movements (e.g. Welsh, Māori) use digital media
B1: a further view, e.g. Crystal: a global lingua franca can coexist with local languages
B1: a reasoned conclusion that follows from the discussion

questions.q: Code-switching is
o: moving between languages or varieties within a conversation
questions.why: Speakers switch for identity, audience or topic.

questions.q: In data analysis, what should be checked against the IPA reference table?
o: The phonemic transcription before commenting on pronunciation
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates misread phonemic symbols instead of checking the table.

questions.q: What is meant by a sociolect?
o: A variety of language used by a social group
questions.why: An idiolect is one person's language.

questions.q: Which term describes the language style unique to one individual?
questions.why: An idiolect is one person's distinctive way of using language. A sociolect belongs to a social group and a dialect to a region.

questions.q: In Communication Accommodation Theory, when speakers adjust their speech to sound more like their listener, this is
questions.why: Convergence reduces social distance and signals approval or belonging. Divergence is making one's speech more different to emphasise distance.

long.q: Explain, with examples, how speakers use code-switching to express identity.
scheme: B1: code-switching: moving between languages or varieties within a conversation
B1: an example, e.g. a British Punjabi speaker switching to Punjabi with grandparents or for in-group jokes
B1: function: signals in-group membership and solidarity
B1: function: marks a change of topic, adds emphasis, or creates distance (e.g. switching to formal English with authority figures)

long.q: Compare the deficit, dominance and difference approaches to language and gender.
scheme: B1: deficit: Lakoff (1975), 'women's language' seen as weaker (hedges, tag questions, empty adjectives, super-polite forms)
B1: criticism: based on introspection and limited data
B1: dominance: Zimmerman and West (1975), men interrupt more in mixed-sex talk, reflecting male power
B1: difference: Tannen, men's 'report talk' (status, information) and women's 'rapport talk' (connection) as different subcultures
B1: criticism of difference: ignores power and overgeneralises
B1: a later approach, e.g. Cameron: gender is performed, and context, role and other factors matter more

long.q: Read this transcript from a workplace meeting. Manager: Right, let's crack on. Sam, figures? Sam: Um, I think they're probably about ten percent up, if that's okay? Manager: Great. Priya, you're on the client call, yeah? Analyse how power is shown in the language of this exchange.
scheme: B1: the manager controls the agenda: the discourse marker 'Right' opens the business and sets the topic
B1: the manager allocates turns by naming speakers ('Sam', 'Priya')
B1: the manager's elliptical, direct forms ('figures?') show little need for politeness, a sign of status
B1: Sam hedges heavily ('Um', 'I think', 'probably', 'if that's okay?'), showing lower status and concern for face
B1: the tag 'yeah?' pushes for agreement rather than asking a real question, linked to a theory (e.g. Fairclough on power in discourse, or Brown and Levinson on face)

long.q: Explain Giles's Communication Accommodation Theory, with an example of convergence and an example of divergence.
scheme: B1: convergence: adjusting speech (accent, speed, lexis) towards the listener's to gain approval or reduce social distance
B1: example, e.g. a job applicant using more standard pronunciation with an interviewer
B1: divergence: emphasising differences in speech to assert identity or increase distance
B1: example, e.g. a speaker broadening their regional accent with a dismissive outsider

long.q: Explain how Labov's department store study linked language to social class, and assess one limitation of the study.
scheme: B1: method: staff in three New York stores of different status were asked a question whose answer was 'fourth floor'
B1: finding: postvocalic /r/ was used most in the highest-status store and least in the lowest
B1: staff used more /r/ when repeating the answer carefully, showing awareness of a prestige form
B1: conclusion: /r/ was a prestige marker, so pronunciation was stratified by social class
B1: a limitation, e.g. class inferred from the store, not from the speaker's own background; only one variable studied
